analysis.one_liner: Creates a nine-agency task force to police and publicly flag for-profit colleges living off federal student aid.
analysis.headline: Six Senate Democrats introduced the bill in March 2026; it has sat in the Senate education committee with no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a committee made up of nine federal agencies — including Education, Justice, the CFPB, the SEC, Defense, and Veterans Affairs — to coordinate oversight and enforcement against for-profit colleges that receive federal student aid. It would set up a single phone line, website, and database for student complaints, require an annual public report on how much federal aid and GI Bill money these schools take in and what students get for it, and publish a yearly warning list naming schools facing fraud suits, sanctions, or waves of borrower-relief claims. For publicly traded for-profit college companies, the report would disclose pre-tax profits, executive pay, and how much revenue goes to recruiting versus teaching.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and prospective students at for-profit colleges, their parents, and veterans spending GI Bill benefits would get a single place to file complaints and a public list of schools facing fraud suits or federal sanctions before they enroll. Taxpayers would get an annual accounting of the federal loans, grants, and military education benefits flowing to the sector, along with default rates, graduation rates, and licensing exam pass rates for each school.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and veterans at for-profit colleges

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a Proprietary Education Interagency Oversight Committee composed of nine federal agencies, charged with improving enforcement, increasing accountability of for-profit colleges to students and taxpayers, and reducing fraud and abuse.

Requires a single toll-free number, website, and database for collecting and routing student complaints about for-profit colleges, with complaints shared among federal agencies and, where appropriate, state regulators.

Requires an annual public report covering federal aid to the sector, graduation and default rates, debt-to-earnings rates, licensing exam pass rates, and enforcement actions taken against each school.

For publicly traded for-profit colleges, requires disclosure of pre-tax profits, executive compensation packages, spending on recruiting and marketing versus instruction, and cost comparisons with public colleges offering the same credentials.

Requires a yearly 'For-Profit College Warning List for Parents and Students' naming schools sued for fraud by federal or state authorities, suspended from federal aid programs, or facing large volumes of borrower-relief claims, with a plain-language explanation and a written response opportunity for each school before publication.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies — especially the publicly traded ones — would bear disclosure of their profits, executive pay, and recruiting spending, school-by-school publication of complaint and enforcement histories, and the reputational cost of appearing on a federal warning list.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates no new enforcement power: it coordinates existing agencies and publishes information, so a school can appear on oversight reports and still keep receiving federal loans, grants, and GI Bill dollars unless an agency acts separately.

The warning list could name schools over pending, unproven allegations — including claims for borrower relief that have not been decided — which could push students away from a school before any finding of wrongdoing; the bill does require letting each school respond in writing before the list is published.
The reporting requirements are extensive, including data broken down by parent company, brand name, and campus, which imposes compliance costs on the institutions being reported on.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency is real: a student or veteran could see a school's profit margins, recruiting spending, complaint history, and default rates before signing up, and nine agencies would finally be required to share what they know. But the bill's weakness is that it informs rather than stops — it does not itself cut off federal aid to schools with poor outcomes, so its value depends on agencies and prospective students actually using the information.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate's education committee, which has taken no further action on it; with the session ending in January 2027, it is on track to die without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced S. 4056 on March 11, 2026, joined by five other Senate Democrats.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the committee's record for the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded for-profit college companies are better off: the coordinated cross-agency enforcement, annual disclosure of their profits and recruiting spending, and a public warning list for students will not happen this session. Students at these schools, meanwhile, go without the complaint system and warning list the bill would have created.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Republican-controlled in this Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the session so far.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee has not acted.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges (proprietary institutions of higher education)
industries.note: These schools would face an annual public report on their federal aid, default rates, complaints, and enforcement history, and a public warning list naming schools sued for fraud or sanctioned. Schools that profit from federal loans, grants, and GI Bill dollars while leaving students with heavy debt and weak job outcomes would lose the low-visibility environment that lets that continue.

The bill's most detailed disclosure targets these companies: pre-tax profit, executive compensation, and the split of revenue between recruiting and instruction, reported per company and brand. That information would let students compare what a school spends to sign them up versus to teach them.

The annual report would name each lender providing private loans at each for-profit college, with borrower counts and dollar volumes. Lending partnerships with high-cost schools would become public, though the bill does not restrict the loans themselves.

Accreditors would be required to share complaint data with federal agencies, and accreditation penalties like probation would appear in the public report. Their gatekeeper role is unchanged, but it becomes more visible.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been in committee for months with no hearing or vote, carries no Republican support, and the session ends in January 2027. Bills at this stage with this level of sponsorship almost never reach the floor; the likely outcome is that it dies at the end of this Congress and would need to be reintroduced in the next one.
